query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The density of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr can be reduced without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures by replacing a portion of the heavier elements (Hf, Ta) with lighter elements (Ti, Zr) while maintaining the high-entropy alloy composition.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g cm−3
generation.intervention: Replace a portion of Hf and Ta with Ti and Zr to form a new high-entropy alloy composition
generation.conditions: Room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 1000 °C
generation.structural_mediator: High-entropy alloy composition with a body-centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure
generation.mechanism: The replacement of heavier elements with lighter elements reduces the overall density of the alloy while maintaining its mechanical properties due to the preservation of the high-entropy alloy composition and BCC crystal structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: The new alloy composition will have a reduced density compared to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr while maintaining its mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g cm−3
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature to 1000 °C; Loading conditions: tensile and compressive loading
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Hf and Ta to be replaced with Ti and Zr to achieve the optimal balance between density reduction and mechanical property preservation is uncertain and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of high-entropy alloy compositions with varying amounts of Hf and Ta replaced with Ti and Zr. Measure the density and mechanical properties (tensile and compressive strength, ductility) of each composition at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 1000 °C.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the new alloy composition exhibits a significant decrease in mechanical properties (tensile and compressive strength, ductility) at room temperature or elevated temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] .
